Al Nayrizi Construction

GeometryConstructionsFractions
Game: See how little marks on two sloping lines can split a segment into equal pieces.
How to play: Drag the dots A, B and C, press + or − to change the number of marks, and tick Show hint to see the equal lengths.
3 marks
Look for the math

Take a segment BC. With a few equally spaced marks on two parallel lines, you can cut BC into exact equal pieces without measuring it at all. Move the points and the cuts follow.

Two lines, the same step

The sloping line through B goes through the point A. Call the step from B to A d. Starting at B, the marks are at B + d, B + 2d, …, B + Nd; the first one is exactly A. Through C we draw a parallel line and step the other way: C − d, C − 2d, …, C − Nd. Both lines now carry N equal steps, but in opposite directions.

Why the joining lines are parallel

Join the i-th mark from B to the (N + 1 − i)-th mark from C. The direction of every one of these lines is

(C − (N + 1 − i) d) − (B + i d) = (C − B) − (N + 1) d

which does not depend on i. So all the joining lines are parallel, and by the intercept theorem they meet the segment BC at equally spaced points, whatever the marks look like.

Which fraction is each cut?

Walk along the line from B + i d. After a fraction i/(N + 1) of the way to its partner, the d part cancels and only BC is left. The cuts are therefore at the exact fractions 1/(N + 1), 2/(N + 1), …, N/(N + 1) of BC. Count the pieces and you get N + 1 equal parts: the logic test checks every N from 1 to 20 and many positions, and compares with the applet's own line-intersection code. The cut-the-knot article says N parts, but its illustration and the original Java applet both show N + 1; the prose here follows what the construction actually does. Moving A changes the marks but never the cuts.

Try dragging A very close to B, then far away: the cuts on BC stay exactly where they were. Press + until you reach 20 marks and watch the fractions change.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
